question: A developer asks an agent for a feature, reads every diff, runs the test suite, and asks the agent to explain a confusing function before merging. Is this vibe coding?
options: Yes: any code written by a model is vibe coding
No: vibe coding means accepting code without reviewing or understanding it; reviewing, testing and owning the result is engineering with an assistant
Yes, because the agent wrote more lines than the developer
Only if the feature is small
explanation: The definition hinges on accountability, not on who typed the code. Simon Willison made this point: not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding.

question: According to the lesson, what is the main practice that lets an agent iterate safely on its own?
options: A longer system prompt
A more expensive model
An automated test suite the agent runs after every change
Asking the agent to be careful
explanation: Tests turn "looks right" into a check the agent can act on. Without them, every iteration needs a human to notice what broke.

question: Which project is a reasonable candidate for vibe coding?
options: A personal script to rename photos on your own laptop, which you will delete next week
The login flow of a customer-facing app
A database migration on production data
An internal tool other teams will depend on
explanation: Vibe code only what is disposable and private, with no production data or credentials in reach. Anything others rely on needs tests, review and an owner.

question: Who proposed the term "agentic engineering" as the name for the disciplined practice?
options: OpenAI, in a model launch announcement
Andrej Karpathy, the developer who had earlier coined "vibe coding"
The OWASP GenAI Security Project
The EU AI Act
explanation: Karpathy coined "vibe coding" and later suggested "agentic engineering"; Simon Willison, who had proposed "vibe engineering", adopted the new term.

question: A team adopts coding agents but has slow, flaky tests and no code review. What does the DORA "amplifier" finding predict?
options: Agents will compensate for the missing practices
Nothing changes: agents have no effect on delivery
AI magnifies existing conditions, so more change volume will hit weak tests and review and likely increase instability
Throughput will fall to zero
explanation: DORA's report frames AI as an amplifier of strengths and dysfunctions; it found AI adoption still associated with lower delivery stability when downstream controls are weak.

question: Which incident illustrates what goes wrong when an agent runs with broad permissions and no harness?
options: An agent on Replit deleting a production database during a code freeze
A model refusing to answer a question
A benchmark score dropping after a model update
A context window being too small
explanation: Destructive actions are a permissions problem: an agent should not hold the ability to delete production data without an approval gate (module 08).
